newsitem.title: italy: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA SEALS ITALIAN SUCCESS STORY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA SEALS ITALIAN SUCCESS STORY.

text.p: Alberto Tomba, seized by his own form of Saturday night fever, left it to the last minute but got what he wanted most at the Alpine skiing world championships -- respect and a medal in Italy.

While compatriot Deborah Compagnoni was hailed as the undisputed queen of the slopes with two golds in slalom and giant slalom that brought her a car as the best skier, the Italian showman struggled in the spotlight.

Repeating the golden double of the 1996 Sierra Nevada championships was always going to be a lot to ask of the triple Olympic champion who has been ill and injured for much of the season and has slipped down the rankings.
Sestriere might or might not have been the 30-year-old Tomba's final fling on the world championships stage and he was determined to put on a good show at home.
After withdrawing from the first leg of the giant slalom on Wednesday, it looked as if he was heading for the loss of face that he dreaded.
But on Saturday, with a remarkable bronze in the slalom behind surprise Norwegian winner Tom Stiansen and France's Sebastien Amiez, Tomba signed off in triumph.
As far as he was concerned, it was worth a gold.
He had been sick and seventh after the first leg, returning to his hotel and summoning a doctor because he felt unwell. Rumours swirled that Tomba would withdraw.
Instead, he went and gave the crowd what it craved, joking later that it was just a "Saturday Night Fever".
The next day's headlines set the seal on what has, for Italy if not Austria, been an outstanding success.
"Bravo Albertone!," said the Gazzetta dello Sport. "Tomba, this bronze is golden," added the Corriere dello Sport.
"I have never felt as much admiration for Alberto Tomba as last night," declared Tuttosport's editor, under the headline "Alberto's pride is stronger than prejudice."
He and downhiller Kristin Ghedina, who also won bronze, were the only Italian men to get medals in Sestriere. The women did the rest with three golds and a silver.
Only the Norwegians, with three men's golds and three silvers, bettered the host nation in the final table.
Atle Skaardal opened the account by retaining his super-G title, just as Italy's Isolde Kostner retained hers.
Kjetil-Andre Aamodt moved closer to overtaking Marc Girardelli, who made a brief appearance only to announce his retirement, as all-time top men's medallist.
Aamodt picked up his 11th career medal in the men's combined, a title previously held by Luxembourg's Girardelli who managed to amass 13 medals over 17 years.
The Austrians, who had been expected to dominate the men's events, failed to live up to expectations.
It was left to Renate Goetschl on the last day to take Austria's only gold in the women's combined.
That was a surprise just as were the two downhills, with Bruno Kernen winning the men's title for Switzerland and Hilary Lindh taking the women's for the United States.
Switzerland's Michael Von Gruenigen, winner of the men's giant, was one of the few favourites to succeed.
Sweden's overall World Cup leader Pernilla Wiberg, with Tomba the other double gold medallist from Sierra Nevada, also left it to the last day to take her medal.
She won a downhill bronze but was delighted with what was her first medal in a speed discipline.
There was a sense of symmetry about Tomba's medal that suggested eerily that his career had come full circle in the resort where he won his first race a decade ago.
The first medal he ever won, 10 years ago, was a bronze at the 1987 Crans Montana championships.

Since then he had never managed to win a world championship medal in an odd year. He won his golds at the 1988 and 1992 Olympics and his only world titles came in an even year after lack of snow forced the 1995 event to be postponed.
"It was a very important medal," Tomba said of his bronze. "After the giant some people stopped believing in me."
